strengths: The paper identifies an important practical bottleneck of diffusion-based generative classifiers and presents a sensible autoregressive alternative with tractable likelihoods.

Partial-scale candidate pruning exploits the coarse-to-fine VAR structure effectively; on ImageNet-100, A-VARC+ attains 89.32% accuracy versus 90.30% for the strongest diffusion classifier while reporting substantially lower inference time.

The ablations separate the effects of likelihood smoothing and CCA fine-tuning, and the analysis honestly reports that VAR classifiers do not inherit the broad distribution-shift robustness previously associated with diffusion classifiers.
Token-level likelihood ratios provide a natural mechanism for class-conditional and contrastive visualizations, with several qualitative successes and failure cases included.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and provides useful subset definitions and pseudocode.
weaknesses: The main techniques have limited novelty: candidate pruning follows an existing coarse-to-fine classification strategy, likelihood smoothing is straightforward Monte Carlo perturbation, and CCA is an existing fine-tuning objective. The principal novelty is therefore the adaptation and empirical study of VAR rather than a substantial methodological advance.

The claimed 160x speedup is insufficiently controlled. Diffusion runtimes are estimated for an A6000 because experiments used heterogeneous hardware, the compared backbones differ substantially, and no matched-hardware latency, throughput, memory, FLOP, or parameter analysis is provided.

Evaluation is small for the strength of the claims: ImageNet-100 contains only 50 examples per class, shifted datasets use only 10 examples per class, and results lack repeated subsets, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Selecting the alphabetically first ten files may also introduce sampling bias.

The explainability claim is supported only qualitatively. There are no comparisons with standard attribution methods, localization or deletion/insertion metrics, human evaluation, or sanity checks establishing faithfulness. The implementation of the unconditional denominator in the token-wise PMI is also not adequately specified.

The catastrophic-forgetting experiment is particularly weak: it covers only ten ImageNet classes and one two-task split, compares against only a naive sequential model and CWR, and lets V-ARC train and retain a separate model for each task. This entails growing parameters and sidesteps rather than directly solves forgetting; likelihood calibration across independently trained models is not analyzed. The claim that arbitrary classifiers trained on different datasets can simply be merged is therefore unsupported.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper points to repositories for underlying components but does not provide its own implementation or enough optimization, fine-tuning, hyperparameter, hardware, and runtime-measurement details to reproduce the central results reliably.

The smoothing definition omits normalization by the number of samples and the statement that computations use log-likelihoods leaves unclear whether the mixture is implemented with the required log-sum-exp or by averaging log-likelihoods, which would constitute a different estimator.

strengths: The paper studies an important practical limitation of generative classifiers: inference cost that scales with both the number of classes and likelihood-estimation expense.
Adapting a visual autoregressive model into a classifier is technically plausible, and partial-scale candidate pruning makes sensible use of the backbone's coarse-to-fine structure.

The main ImageNet-100 results show a promising accuracy-efficiency trade-off relative to the evaluated generative baselines, while the ablation separates the effects of likelihood smoothing and CCA fine-tuning.
The paper is generally understandable and commendably reports that VAR-based classification does not reproduce most of the distribution-shift robustness attributed to diffusion classifiers.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Direct likelihood classification is a standard generative-classification construction; multistage candidate pruning and likelihood smoothing are familiar strategies; and CCA is taken from prior work. The contribution is primarily a combination of existing ideas around a new backbone rather than a substantial algorithmic advance.

The headline 160x speedup is not established under a controlled benchmark. Diffusion runtime is estimated for an A6000 because experiments used heterogeneous hardware, while the hardware and measurement protocol for the proposed method are insufficiently documented. End-to-end memory, throughput, batching, preprocessing, and variance are also absent.

The evaluation is too small for the breadth of the claims. ImageNet-100 uses only 50 examples per class, shifted datasets use only 10 examples per class selected largely by filename order, and no confidence intervals, repeated samples, or full-dataset results are reported. Calling this a comprehensive analysis is therefore not justified.

The explainability claim is supported only by selected qualitative heatmaps. There are no comparisons to established attribution methods, quantitative localization or faithfulness tests, deletion/insertion experiments, sanity checks, or user studies. The construction and spatial aggregation of the unconditional token likelihoods also need more implementation detail.

The catastrophic-forgetting experiment is not a convincing continual-learning comparison. VARC+ trains two separate models independently, whereas ResNet is forced to update a single model sequentially. This avoids forgetting by expanding model and training cost and assumes that independently trained likelihoods are comparable. Appropriate baselines—such as separate discriminative experts, parameter-expansion methods, replay methods, and stronger continual-learning algorithms—are missing. The experiment covers only ten classes and two tasks, so the broad claim of inherent resistance is overstated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper supplies pseudocode and links to component repositories but does not provide the proposed system's code or checkpoints, complete hardware and batching details, training costs, random seeds, or sufficient detail for reproducing PMI maps and runtime measurements.

The proposed classifier remains substantially worse than standard discriminative models in both accuracy and speed. Its claimed practical applicability is therefore demonstrated only relative to other costly generative classifiers, not relative to realistic classification alternatives.

Several important sensitivities are missing, including pruning-stage choices, candidate counts, smoothing variance and sample count, calibration across class-conditional models, and the effect of pruning on different shifts. Overall, the work contains a potentially useful empirical observation, but the novelty and evidence are insufficient for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper explores a timely and comparatively underexamined direction: using visual autoregressive models as generative classifiers. Exploiting VAR's tractable token likelihood and multiscale structure is well motivated.
A-VARC+ achieves an appealing accuracy-efficiency trade-off on ImageNet-100: 89.32% accuracy versus 90.30% for the stronger diffusion classifier while reporting roughly 160x lower inference time.

The likelihood smoothing and partial-scale pruning ideas are intuitive and practically useful, while the discussion of the trade-off between generative quality and classification accuracy provides a valuable empirical observation.
The study does not conceal negative findings: it shows that the distribution-shift robustness associated with diffusion classifiers generally does not transfer to VAR classifiers.
The paper is clearly organized and includes helpful pseudocode, dataset-class lists, ablations for smoothing and CCA, qualitative explanations, and failure-case visualizations.
weaknesses: The scalability claim is not adequately demonstrated. Experiments use only ImageNet-100, and shifted-dataset evaluations use just 10 deterministically selected images per class. No ImageNet-1K experiment establishes that pruning remains accurate or that the method is practical at the scale motivating the work.

The headline 160x speedup is not based on a clean controlled benchmark: diffusion runtime is estimated for an A6000 because experiments used heterogeneous hardware. Hardware, batching, precision, preprocessing, and memory details are insufficient for a reliable efficiency comparison.

The methodological novelty is moderate. A-VARC largely combines direct autoregressive likelihood evaluation with Monte Carlo smoothing, staged candidate pruning, and the previously proposed CCA objective. The paper lacks an isolated ablation quantifying the accuracy-speed effect of partial-scale pruning and sensitivity to stage counts, retained candidates, scale cutoffs, and smoothing noise.

The explainability claim is supported only by selected qualitative heatmaps. There are no comparisons with standard attribution methods, quantitative localization or faithfulness metrics, deletion/insertion tests, human evaluation, or sanity checks demonstrating that the maps causally reflect the classifier's decisions.

The catastrophic-forgetting experiment is too weak to support the stated inherent-resistance claim. It covers only 10 classes and two tasks, while VARC+ trains and retains an independent model for each task. This avoids parameter interference by increasing storage rather than solving continual learning under a comparable fixed-memory budget; stronger rehearsal-free baselines and a joint-training upper bound are also absent.

Results are reported without multiple runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is especially problematic for the small distribution-shift subsets and for conclusions drawn from differences of only a few points.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the paper points to repositories for constituent models but does not provide an implementation of A-VARC+, and several training, runtime-measurement, and compute-budget details needed to reproduce the main results are missing.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical limitation of diffusion-based generative classifiers and shows that the tractable likelihood and multiscale structure of visual autoregressive models can reduce classification cost substantially. The reported 89x GFLOP reduction relative to the two-stage DiT classifier, at less than one percentage point lower ImageNet-100 accuracy, is compelling within the generative-classifier setting.

The proposed system is technically coherent: likelihood smoothing addresses instability from discrete tokenization, partial-scale pruning exploits the VAR architecture naturally, and CCA strengthens class-conditional information. Ablations support the accuracy gains from smoothing and CCA and examine relevant hyperparameters.

The evaluation covers several generative model families, discriminative baselines, and multiple distribution-shift datasets. The negative finding that VAR classifiers do not inherit the broad robustness of diffusion classifiers is useful and is presented candidly.

Token-wise mutual information is an appealing, computationally efficient use of autoregressive likelihood decomposition. The paper provides qualitative examples, comparisons against LIME and SHAP, and insertion/deletion measurements rather than relying only on visualizations.
weaknesses: The main techniques are largely combinations or direct adaptations of established ideas: Monte Carlo smoothing, coarse-to-fine candidate pruning, and previously proposed CCA fine-tuning. Using a tractable autoregressive likelihood for classification is natural, so the methodological novelty is moderate.

The evaluation is too small for several central conclusions. ImageNet-100 contains only 5,000 test examples, distribution-shift results use merely 10 examples per class, and no confidence intervals, repeated subsamples, or statistical tests are reported. Small differences such as those in the explanation results are therefore difficult to interpret.

The efficiency evidence relies only on theoretical GFLOPs. Wall-clock latency, throughput, peak memory, tokenization overhead, and hardware-dependent batching behavior are absent. Moreover, A-VARC+ still costs 4,649 GFLOPs per image—orders of magnitude more than the discriminative models—so claims of substantially improved practical usability should be qualified.

Candidate pruning lacks a clean end-to-end ablation varying the number of retained candidates and stages while reporting final top-1 accuracy and total cost. The partial-scale study primarily reports top-10 retention, making it hard to isolate pruning's contribution and understand its failure modes.

The explainability evaluation is potentially circular. Insertion and deletion are approximated by masking and summing precomputed token log-likelihoods rather than rerunning the model on genuinely modified inputs or sequences. This evaluates faithfulness to the chosen additive likelihood decomposition and may structurally favor TMI; the paper also provides no localization-based or human-grounded evaluation.

The class-incremental experiment is not a fair comparison: A-VARC+ and the diffusion classifier train a separate full model for each task and merge their likelihoods, thereby increasing capacity and storage, whereas the discriminative baseline updates one model sequentially. Avoiding forgetting under independent per-task models is largely expected and previously established. Testing only two five-class tasks is insufficient to support broad class-incremental-learning claims.

A-VARC+ remains below standard discriminative classifiers in accuracy while being vastly more expensive, and it shows no general distribution-shift advantage. Thus its practical significance beyond serving as a more efficient generative-classifier baseline is presently limited.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the stated implementation URL is an empty placeholder, and several implementation choices needed to reproduce training, likelihood computation, and GFLOP accounting are not fully specified.

strengths: The manuscript studies a timely practical limitation of generative classification and shows that VAR's tractable likelihood can make inference substantially cheaper than diffusion-based classification.

The multi-scale candidate-pruning idea is well matched to the VAR architecture, and A-VARC+ achieves 89.32% on ImageNet-100 versus 90.30% for the two-stage diffusion classifier at roughly 89x lower reported GFLOPs.

The paper includes useful ablations of smoothing sample count, noise variance, CCA fine-tuning, and model scale. It also candidly reports that most distribution-shift robustness attributed to diffusion classifiers does not transfer to VAR.

The exploration of token-level likelihood attribution and class-incremental learning identifies potentially useful research directions, and the manuscript is generally organized and visually clear. weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The main ingredients are latent-noise likelihood smoothing, coarse-to-fine candidate pruning, and an existing CCA objective. Their integration is sensible, but it does not amount to a substantial new learning method or theoretical contribution.

The practical-efficiency framing is overstated. A-VARC+ still requires 4,649 GFLOPs per image—roughly 275x the reported cost of ViT-B/16—while attaining lower accuracy. The headline 89x reduction is relative to an exceptionally expensive diffusion procedure; no wall-clock latency, memory, throughput, batching, or hardware measurements are provided.

The evaluation is too small and statistically weak for several claims. Distribution-shift results use only 10 examples per class, selected partly by filename order, with no confidence intervals or repeated trials. Full ImageNet-1K accuracy and scaling behavior are absent despite scalability being a central motivation.

The explainability evaluation is questionable. Insertion and deletion are computed by masking precomputed token log-likelihood terms rather than rerunning the model on genuinely modified inputs. This surrogate is closely aligned with the proposed likelihood-based attribution and does not establish faithfulness to actual model behavior. TMI also loses substantially to LIME before CCA and beats the baselines only narrowly afterward, without uncertainty estimates, sanity checks, localization benchmarks, or human evaluation.

The class-incremental experiment is not a fair demonstration of avoiding catastrophic forgetting: the generative approach trains and retains separate models independently for each task, whereas the main discriminative baseline updates one model sequentially. This avoids forgetting largely by construction while increasing model storage with the number of tasks. The experiment covers only two five-class tasks and omits strong modern continual-learning baselines and resource accounting.

The likelihood-smoothing definition and implementation are underspecified. Equation 9 presents an unnormalized sum of probabilities, while the appendix says computations use log-likelihoods without explaining whether log-sum-exp is used. Details needed to reproduce the unconditional likelihood used by TMI and several training or fine-tuning settings are also incomplete.

Overall, the paper contains an interesting empirical observation and engineering direction, but the limited novelty and major weaknesses in the explainability and continual-learning evidence prevent the broader central claims from being adequately supported at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical limitation of diffusion-based generative classifiers and presents a clear alternative based on VAR models with tractable likelihoods.
A-VARC combines sensible techniques—latent-space likelihood smoothing and partial-scale candidate pruning—and the ablations substantiate their respective accuracy and efficiency effects.

The principal efficiency result is compelling within the generative-classifier setting: A-VARC+ approaches the two-stage DiT classifier on ImageNet-100 (89.32% versus 90.30%) while reducing inference cost by approximately 89×.

The empirical comparison covers several model families and five distribution shifts. The paper also reports negative findings transparently, notably that VAR-based classification does not inherit the broad distribution-shift robustness attributed to diffusion classifiers.

The token-wise mutual-information explanation is natural for an autoregressive likelihood model, computationally attractive, and supported by quantitative comparisons and useful qualitative examples, including failure cases.

The paper is clearly written and supplies algorithmic details, dataset class lists, hyperparameter ablations, and a discussion of the trade-off between generative quality and classification performance.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: candidate pruning and smoothing are relatively straightforward, while CCA is an existing finetuning objective. The main contribution is therefore primarily the integration and empirical study of these components for VAR classification.

The headline efficiency comparison is favorable only relative to diffusion generative classifiers. A-VARC+ still requires 4,649 GFLOPs per image, while discriminative baselines are both substantially cheaper and generally more accurate; this limits the immediate practical-use claim.

Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-100 rather than full ImageNet-1K, even though scaling with the number of classes is the central motivation. Shift evaluations further use only ten deterministically selected examples per class, with no confidence intervals or repeated subsampling, weakening the robustness conclusions.

The class-incremental experiment is only a ten-class, two-task proof of concept. Training and retaining an independent model for each task avoids parameter interference by construction and introduces growing storage cost; calibration of likelihoods across independently trained models is not studied. Thus, the evidence does not yet support broad claims about continual learning or arbitrarily merging classifiers.

The explainability evaluation uses precomputed token log-likelihoods and simulates insertion/deletion by masking terms in their sum rather than modifying the model input. This is closely aligned with how TMI is constructed and may favor likelihood-based attributions; comparison against localization annotations or input-level perturbation tests would provide stronger external validation.

The paper reports single results without variance across seeds, sensitivity of the full multistage pipeline, or a fuller end-to-end accuracy–compute Pareto curve. It is also unclear whether smoothing and pruning hyperparameters were selected using a separate validation set.
